works.description:
**Note:** Chapter One: The Never-Ending Dunes and The Wondering Xandrixes.

---
Introduction

…I stood upon the edge of the abyss. The cold bit at my skin as the dark mist swelled around me and overhead. I stared into the darkness, straining my eyes to glimpse something… anything. I stayed motionless for some time, praying that I might see some sign of hope, but no. For in the great darkness, no light can be found…

Books lined the shelves. They covered the floors and tables. Some could even be found in the pantries alongside outlandish fares like goblin's eyes or Ogers’ tongue, all kept bobbing and floating neatly in sealed jars for later consumption. The sun peered in through an open window, and off in the distance, a peculiar cuckoo clock cooed. As the sunbeams stretched across the floor like growing vines of light, they began to touch upon the face of one bizarre creature. Eyes fast shut, holding back golden orbs ornately chiseled by deep brown irises and large, seamlessly bottomless pupils. His pale green skin glistened like sea froth at the first peak of the morning, contrasted by the dark shadows of his room. His limbs, elegant and elongated, lay sprawled about the bed as he wiped his eyes. As he rose, his frame towered above the furnishings in his room; though thin, he stood at almost 8 feet in stature. However, he may not be easily defined by his features or flowing dark locks.

This elf, who goes by the name “Elaris Sel Marden,” or for short Elaris, was prized with the duty to oversee and protect the temple’s contents and ensure that no ill fate becomes the worlds that lie within. works.description: Elaris thumbed through a series of books as he savored a bit of roast sea lizard. “Since I am enshrined in this place for eternity, I might as well come to love what I am protecting,” he mumbled with a full mouth. Elaris picked up a plain-looking book with sand on the cover and sifting out through its pages. He turned it over to find the name, but there wasn’t one. “ Well, I guess since this one doesn’t have a name, I’ll just have to read this one and find out what to call it,” he thought to himself. He decided he would leave the book on the table next to a chair and find a cup of tea to enjoy while he was reading. Elaris was trying to make the best of his situation. He had not chosen to become a scholar for the rest of his life, but things had happened that had made this his permanent occupation. He was never to leave, and he could only be replaced when he had died. A small part of him wished not to be here, but this was an honor and a much better outcome than he deserved. In the pantry, Elaris searched for what he thought to be the most suitable tea to go with his morning readings. He pushed aside one last container until he found the one he sought. It was mint herbal tea with a unique herb in it that made scholars more vividly imagine, if not envision, the book they were reading so clearly it was as if they were the narrator of the book. Now sitting in his chair and sipping his tea, he opened the book and began to read.

works.description: My ear rang loudly, and I could feel the blood pulsing to it—one of the shamans had hit me with his cane. “We do not ride on the backs of the gods. You will be punished if we hear much more nonsense from you, Xandri.” The head shaman, Xadra, warned. I was pulled out of the crowd and taken somewhere more secluded. Another one of the shamans gave the same speech I always get. It always leads back to how I’m the son of the great explorer and should be a better example to my peers who needed someone to look up to, but I didn’t care to be the babysitter for my tribe; I wanted to explore as my father did and none of these people could stop me. I came back to reality after zoning out as I often did. The last thing I heard, and the only thing I heard, was, “I expected a better offspring from someone as great as your father.” I rolled my eyes and wondered what it must have been like to be my father. He had the same experiences I had with the tribes-people. They all held him back, keeping him from his potential until he proved himself. I had to prove myself.

works.description: Later that night, Xandri lay awake in his room. He stared at the ceiling and thought in silence until, finally, he had come to a resolve. He would traverse the desert and not return until he found the end. He jumped out of his bed and grabbed his pack covered in holes and bits of scant patchwork that was coming apart at the seams. His father, though significant, didn’t leave him much. They were poor, and his father’s death had left him poorer. His mother died in childbearing; he was lucky he hadn’t died with her. After packing, he walked to the mirror and cleaned himself with water from a pitcher. His skin was dark from many years under the sun and full of scales. His clan were descendants of lizards that had lived in the desert. It was said that the Xandrixes had blessed them with their human form so they may worship them and that they would turn them back to lizards if they stopped. Xandri, like his father, struggled to believe that genuinely divine creatures would be so callous.

works.description:
WrymWretch

Story plot line  
ACT I — READER‑READY NARRATIVE

The first sign came quietly, the way rot always does—soft, almost apologetic, as if asking permission to exist. Thalen of Cedarheart noticed it while tracking a silver‑antlered stag through the western groves. The forest should have been humming with life, but the air felt thin, as though something had taken a long breath and forgotten to exhale.

He found the tree at the edge of a clearing. Its trunk had split open from within, not by lightning or age, but by something that pulsed like a second heartbeat. Black ichor seeped from the wound, thick and slow, and when it touched the moss, the moss turned gray and brittle, collapsing into dust that didn’t even remember how to be soil.

works.title: Passage 2
works.description:
Thalen reached out. The tree recoiled—not in movement, but in spirit. A shiver ran through him, a sensation like brushing against a memory that wasn’t his. He stumbled back, heart pounding, and for a moment he thought he heard a whisper beneath the bark, a voice trying to form a name it no longer possessed.

He ran. Branches clawed at him as he sprinted toward the outpost, and the forest seemed to lean away from him, as if ashamed of what it had shown. By the time he burst through the wooden gates, he could barely speak.

“The forest is… forgetting,” he managed. “Something is making it forget.”

The rangers exchanged uneasy glances. They had heard rumors. None dared speak the name behind them.

Not yet.

Far to the north, where the sky‑cities drifted like pale islands in the clouds, Lady Aeris Galewing stood on her balcony and watched her people tremble. Sky Elves were not meant to shiver. Their bodies were tuned to the cold, their minds sharp as the winds they commanded. Yet now they lay wrapped in blankets, wings drooping, eyes unfocused.

A healer approached her, his voice barely above a whisper. “They speak of voices in the wind. They say the stars are calling them by name.”

Aeris had heard the voices too. Soft at first, then insistent. A whisper threading through the clouds: Remember me.

The Priests of the Gale summoned her to the storm chamber. Lightning flickered across the crystalline walls as they spoke of omens, of sickness, of something brushing against the minds of the living. Aeris was chosen to descend from the sky and seek aid from the other realms.

As she prepared her sky‑sail, she looked once more at her people—fevered, trembling, whispering to unseen stars. Something ancient was stirring, and it was reaching for them.

In the deep southern forests, Elder Rhyla Mosswhisper knelt before the Heartstone. The crystal’s glow, once steady as the earth’s pulse, flickered like a dying ember. She placed her palms upon it, and a tremor ran through her bones.

works.title: Passage 4
works.description:
The vision struck her like a blow: a prison without walls, a name dissolving into silence, a cosmic shape pressing against the veil of existence. She gasped and pulled her hands away. The Heartstone dimmed further, as though exhausted by the effort of remembering.

“Not yet,” she whispered. “You cannot fade. Not now.”

But the crystal knew the truth. Its power was tied to memory, and memory was being erased.

Rhyla rose, leaning heavily on her staff. She would journey to the Deep Core, where the oldest crystals slept. If any wisdom remained, it would be there.

Along the eastern shores, Lunessa Tidecaller waded into water that should have been alive with darting fish and swirling light. Instead, the sea lay still—murky, heavy, suffocating. She dipped her hand beneath the surface, and the water clung to her skin like oil.

Behind her, the elders murmured in fear. The ocean was losing its memory of life.

She surfaced screaming.

In the Underworld, Kael Duskbane pushed open the stone door of the forbidden chamber. Dust swirled. Candles flared. The prophecy lay open on a pedestal of bone.

When the last memory fades, the Astral Architect shall rise.

Kael’s blood ran cold. He had heard the name once, whispered by a dying sage: Shallock Izladar. A name the world was trying to forget.

He closed the tome and drew his blade. Someone was erasing memories. Someone was killing witnesses.

Kael would hunt them.

The night after the forest’s first forgetting, Thalen could not sleep. The Cedarheart Enclave was restless; even the leaves seemed to whisper in uneasy spirals. Sylvan lay coiled beneath the great elder‑tree, its massive form half‑hidden by vines that grew and shifted with its breath. The dragon’s presence steadied the forest, but only barely. The corruption pulsed at the edges of the grove like a bruise.

Thalen sat beside Sylvan’s flank, feeling the warmth of the dragon’s heartbeat through the bark‑like scales. His own pulse matched it, as it always had. He had known since childhood that he was different — that the forest spoke to him in ways it didn’t to others, that vines curled toward his hands, that animals watched him with knowing eyes. But he had never understood why.

He set it aside and pushed himself upright, the familiar ache of a seasoned hangover settling behind his eyes. This was not the clumsy rise of a novice drunk; this was the practiced, almost graceful ascent of a man who had greeted many dawns in this exact condition.

The light outside was shifting. Thin threads of orange stretched across the porthole, weaving themselves into the gold of early morning. He blinked at it, squinting as though the sun were an adversary he had not prepared to face.

With a soft groan, he stood and made his way through the cluttered cabin, stepping over scattered notes and half‑finished sketches. The stairs creaked beneath his weight as he climbed to the deck.

The world greeted him with a hush.

The sea was calm, a pane of molten gold reflecting the newborn sky. The shoreline lay not far off—a quiet crescent of pale sand, untouched and waiting. He stared at it with bleary, unfocused eyes, as though trying to remember why it mattered. Something in him stirred. A pull. A promise he couldn’t name.

Before he could think better of it, he swung himself over the rail and dropped into the dinghy tied alongside. The small boat rocked, then steadied. He took up the oars with the muscle memory of a man who had crossed many uncertain waters, and began to row.

The journey was short, but each stroke felt like a negotiation with the remnants of last night’s rum. The dinghy slid onto the sand with a soft, wet squelch. He stepped out, boots sinking slightly into the cool grit.

He walked toward the place where the tide kissed the shore—a narrow, shimmering boundary between sea and land. The air there felt different, charged with something he couldn’t name. He paused, letting the waves lap at his ankles, letting the morning settle around him.

works.description:
His feet sank into the sand with a wet, sucking sound, each step a slow negotiation with the earth. My toes—his toes—had long since grown rough from the constant embrace of salt and grit, the sea forever sculpting them into something less human and more… tidal. He trudged forward with the heavy, deliberate gait of a man who had only recently remembered he possessed legs at all. The tide had retreated moments before, leaving the beach slick and gleaming, as though he were walking across the exposed ribs of the ocean itself.

Then came the voice.

“Alexi!”

Smooth. Sweet. Too clean for this wild place. It drifted over the tropical wind like a ribbon of perfume—synthetic pineapple and coconut, the unmistakable scent of someone who had never once applied her own sunscreen. Even the breeze carried the memory of hands that had rubbed lotion into royal shoulders.

He turned toward it, blinking through the haze of rum and morning light. And then—because instinct is faster than thought—he rushed toward the sound.

works.description:
Well, “rushed” is generous. He lurched. He zigzagged. He performed what future scholars might generously describe as a bold and experimental interpretation of running. But he moved with purpose, and that counts for something.

He stopped a little too late.

Which is to say: he didn’t stop at all.

He collided with her—a small, startled figure in a pale dress—and the two of them went down in a tangle of limbs, sand, and royal disbelief. Her dress, once pristine, now bore the full signature of the beach. And some say his hands, in the chaos of the fall, traveled further than any man’s had before—for she was a princess, after all, and princesses are not accustomed to being tackled by hungover sailors at dawn.

He scrambled backward, found his balance, lost it again, and collapsed into something that might have been a bow, or a grovel, or a man attempting to fold himself into a shape the gods would find amusing.

“Everything has a lord,” she said. “But this one… he is hungry. He wants every ship, every vessel, every soul that sails. He wants to turn the ocean into his fleet. He will drain the empire, and then the people, until all that remains is a wasteland of scraps and ash.”

The wind shifted. The scent of pineapple faded. Something colder took its place.

Alexi felt the weight settle on him—not the weight of her words, but the weight of what they meant. The world tilting. The tide pulling back. The kind of moment a man remembers long after he has forgotten his own name.

He imagined a life without the sea.

A life where no one knew the warm blush of sunrise over open water.  
Where no one tasted the salt on the rim of a bottle weathered by storms.  
Where no one sang drunken hymns to the tide, praising her like a lover who always returned.  
Where the ocean was not a wild, living thing—but a factory, a fleet, a machine.

His phone chimed as a text popped onto the screen. Daniel glanced at the message; he was the new student at a prestigious college known for its exceptional education and… wild parties. The message read: “Don’t be boring, Daniel. We hate boring. Party this weekend. Be there.” Daniel let out a sigh. Parties and their associated activities were not his cup of tea. He had always been a bookworm, dedicating himself to maintaining good grades to secure a promising career like his father. His father had always discouraged him from reckless behavior and he did whatever his father told him to, but maybe this time it could be different?

If he stayed in his room, he was the creep. If he went, he risked his father’s disappointment. Either way, he was trapped. Finally, he decided: “What harm could it do? I’ll give it a try.”

The following days passed swiftly, and Daniel was getting ready for the upcoming party in his private dorm room. Thanks to his father’s extra payment, he didn’t have to deal with a lousy roommate who might “influence him negatively” according to his father. As he glanced at himself in the mirror, he couldn’t help but feel self-conscious. His scrawny frame, thin shoulders and ill-fitting glasses epitomized the image of a social outcast. Contemplating a change, he removed his glasses, hoping they might enhance his appearance and make him seem cooler. Though it meant sacrificing clear vision, Daniel reassured himself: “It’ll be fine. What’s the worst that can happen?”

The music could’ve been heard from 3 blocks down. Nervousness hit Daniel as he climbed the steps of the frat house, neon lights flickering like warning signs through dingy curtained windows. The booming music echoed disrupting his heartbeat. Suddenly the door flung open, a drunk student stumbles out the door and vomits over the railing, losing his balance and tumbling into the bushes. Daniel froze, ready to bolt at the sight —until strong hands grabbed him.

works.title: Passage 3
works.description:
Matty, the lively girl who had texted him, smiled too wide. Her eyes lingered on him, measuring. Ralph her boyfriend, stood towering next to her, his hulking frame sending fear through Daniel. Ralph’s grip on his shoulders was uncomfortably tight but Matty’s words were worse, “You weren’t thinking about leaving, were you?” Matty teased.  
“No,” Daniel lied.  
“Good. We hate quitters. Now come inside and let’s get this night started.” Matty said with a blissful tone.

Inside, the party was chaos. Blaring music. Students chanting “chug, chug, chug.” Lines of cocaine on tables. Smoke so thick it made Daniel choke. Dealers handed out handfuls of loose pills like candy. Daniel’s stomach turned. Report it, and he’d be a snitch. Leave, and he’d be a loser. Stay, and maybe he’d finally belong.

Matty shoved a red solo cup into his hand. “Drink.”  
He gulped, vodka, his throat burned but the warmth spread. Another cup followed—sweet, syrupy, strange. His body hummed, light as air, his mind started moving slower.

works.title: Passage 4
works.description:
Walls dripped like wax. Faces melted into grotesque masks, whispering his name. He reached for his glasses, but they were gone. How could he see without them, now the blur became monstrous—colors bleeding, shadows twisting. He was just trying to keep it calm, cool, collected. Then all of a sudden, Matty appeared again, a few blotter tabs in her palm, mixed with a few red and white pills. Matty didn’t take any. 
“Open up,” she said.  
He paused.  
“I said open up!” Her tone was menacing and Daniel was too far out of it to think for himself right now. 
So, He obeyed.

The world fractured. His heartbeat thundered, then slowed to a crawl. The floor rippled beneath him. His own hands looked alien, melting into the couch. His breathe seemed to hitch, the corners of his mouth felt locked, his stomached churning.

Matty leaned close, her lips brushing his ear as her words cut sharp:  
“You’re done, Daniel. No books. No daddy’s money. Just you—foaming, choking, dying. I’m gonna watch as you suffer and I’m gonna enjoy it.” She almost giggled with this last part. Daniel was in horror, he thought Matty was his friend now he knew otherwise.

works.title: Passage 5
works.description:
He collapsed, convulsing, froth spilling from his lips. The room warped into endless corridors, each echoing his father’s disappointed face.

Dawn came and police lights flickered outside the frat house. Daniel’s body was hauled onto a stretcher, barely hanging on.

“Officer, I found him like this,” Matty said, voice trembling with false concern. “Will he be alright, I would hate for anything to happen to him” she said faking a whimper of sadness. 
The officer just nodded, commending her bravery, and said “ there isn’t anything we can do, these kids aren’t going to listen, they’ll just keep doing this stuff. So trust me, he won’t be the last. Just stay safe and keep out of trouble.” The officer left and Matty stood there alone in front of the frat house stairs watching as they left on the ambulance. She smiled politely but inside, her sick satisfaction bloomed. As the ambulance doors shut, her phone buzzed again. Another name lit the screen. Another lamb.

Missing Campsites: A Slow-Burn Horror Mystery About Vanishing Reality

Imagine arriving at a remote campground only to discover something is… off.

Not dangerous.  
Not dramatic.  
Just wrong.

In Missing Campsites, a group of campers pulls into a national forest expecting a quiet weekend. But the first few campsites — the ones that should be right there at the entrance — simply aren’t. Not destroyed. Not taped off. Not overgrown.

They just don’t exist.

The map shows them.  
The signs point to them.  
But the land is empty.

The campers are unsettled, but everyone else — rangers, families, hikers — acts like nothing is missing.

The next morning, more campsites have vanished.

No one notices.  
No one cares.  
No one even remembers they were there.

Except the campers.

By the end of the second day, the entire campground has been erased from reality — all except the last five sites, the ones where the campers are staying. They’re now the only fixed points in a landscape that’s quietly unraveling.

Shaun went to the front desk, where he was handed a sheet to fill out before his interview. The questions on the sheet were unusual, delving into personal information like his birthplace and background. Though uncomfortable, he reluctantly filled it out.

Returning the sheet to the receptionist, Shaun noticed her blank expression, as if something was amiss. She took the sheet from him and swiftly pricked his finger, collecting a blood sample. Startled, Shaun recoiled and demanded answers, his voice a mix of rage and fear. The receptionist remained impassive and pointed towards a set of large double doors. "It's just a crazy coincidence," he reassured himself quietly as he pushed through the doors and entered the lobby.

Inside, an emblem on the floor caught his attention—a snake devouring a lion. It was a logo unlike any he had seen before, piquing his curiosity. Suddenly, a receptionist called his name over the speakers. The speakers emitted a hissing sound before abruptly cutting off. Shaun went to the front desk, where he was handed a sheet to fill out before his interview. The questions on the sheet were unusual, delving into personal information like his birthplace and background. Though uncomfortable, he reluctantly filled it out.

Returning the sheet to the receptionist, Shaun noticed her blank expression, as if something was amiss. She took the sheet from him and swiftly pricked his finger, collecting a blood sample. Startled, Shaun recoiled and demanded answers, his voice a mix of rage and fear. The receptionist remained impassive and pointed towards a set of large double doors. Hesitant, he approached them, realizing that aside from the receptionist, he was the only person in the building. Puzzled, he wondered why a large corporation would have so few people present.

works.title: Passage 1
works.description:
The Yellow Drop and The Plain Before Sound

In the first morning, the ear held only a pale, waiting surface — a blank stretch of nothing that felt more like potential than space.

Then a yellow drop of sound fell.

It struck the emptiness and rippled outward in warm, trembling rings, the way the first stir of wind might ripple across a still lake. The ripple brightened the plain, hinting at depth, hinting at direction, as if the world were remembering how to begin.

A second sound followed — a high, feather‑light note that fluttered across the ripples like a bird testing the air.  
Then a deeper tone arrived, slow and weighted, settling into the ground like packed earth.  
A bright, sharp chime cracked through the space, breaking open the horizon the way a wave breaks against stone.

works.title: Passage 2
works.description:
They fell at irregular intervals, like a hesitant composer testing notes in an empty hall.  
Each one a different shade of sound — thin silver ticks, dull red thuds, pale blue hums — spreading outward, overlapping, interfering.  
Where they crossed, new patterns formed: soft oscillations, trembling grids, invisible architecture.

This was not light painting a scene.  
This was sound building one.

High notes lifted the air, giving it height.  
Low notes thickened the ground, giving it weight.  
Mid‑tones stretched themselves into long, trembling lines that became the first hints of structure — arches of resonance, pillars of vibration, corridors made of nothing but pressure and rhythm.

The soundscape grew more intricate.  
The air thickened with tone.  
The ground hummed with quiet intention.

And still, the yellow drop kept falling.

Each drip struck the forming landscape with a steady, patient rhythm.  
Each one added a new layer of motion.  
Each one deepened the sense that something was gathering itself, preparing to become.

works.title: Passage 3
works.description:
The rhythm quickened — not frantic, but inevitable, like a tide rising toward shore.  
The whole sound‑world leaned forward, trembling at the edge of revelation.

Then the final drop fell — bright, sharp, impossibly clear.

And the body opened its eyes.

The sound‑architecture collapsed in an instant, folding back into silence.  
The ripples flattened.  
The spires dissolved.  
The trembling ground became nothing more than sensation.

The point of view slid outward, smooth as breath — from the ear’s inner creation to the dim room beyond the eyelids.

We see now through the body’s eyes.

The alarm is buzzing.  
The morning has begun.  
But for a heartbeat, the echo of that sound‑born world lingers — the memory of a universe that rose and fell in the space between dreaming and waking.

A Journey Into the Heartstream: The Rite of the Blue‑Born

This chapter follows the Blue‑Born, a people who grow inside the marrow caverns of the bones. Their skin is pigmented a deep, mineral blue — the color of uncirculated blood, the color of youth before recognition.

They live in a labyrinth of glowing marrow tunnels, where the walls pulse faintly with the rhythm of the distant heart. Their society is calm, cold, and ceremonial. Everything they do prepares them for the moment they will leave the bones forever.

That moment is called The Recognition.

🦴 The Age of Recognition

When a Blue‑Born reaches adulthood, their pigment begins to fade — not to pale, but to red, the color of circulation. It is the body’s way of calling them upward.

works.title: Passage 2
works.description:
The elders gather.  
The marrow lights dim.  
The cavern hums with the pulse of the heart.

The young men stand together, trembling not with fear but with the weight of inevitability. They have grown up side by side, carved tools together, sung marrow‑songs together, dreamed of the world above the bone.

Now they must leave it.

🚣 The Ascent to the Bloodstream

A narrow shaft opens in the bone — a vertical tunnel lined with soft, living tissue. The Blue‑Born climb, feeling the temperature rise, feeling the pulse grow louder.

At the top, they emerge into the Bloodstream.

It is not a tube.  
It is a river.

A vast, winding, crimson waterway that coils through the body like the Amazon. The current is strong. The air is humid and metallic. Strange creatures lurk beneath the surface — translucent predators shaped like cells, drifting tendrils that sting, massive immune beasts that patrol the waters.

works.title: Passage 3
works.description:
Waiting for them is the Ceremonial Raft — a living vessel grown from tissue, shaped by tradition, guided by instinct.

They board together, still a brotherhood.

They do not know how long that will last.

🌧️ The River of Blood

The raft drifts through the bloodstream, carried by the pulse. The journey is beautiful and terrifying:

• towering artery walls rise like canyon cliffs  
• branching vessels split like river deltas  
• swirling eddies pull at the raft  
• immune creatures watch from the shadows

The young men laugh, argue, dream, and fear — all the emotions of early adulthood, amplified by the knowledge that this is the last time they will ever be together.

The river grows narrower.  
The current grows faster.  
The heart draws near.

❤️ The Heart of the Body

The heart is not a chamber.  
It is a cathedral.

A massive, thundering structure of muscle and light, beating with ancient purpose. The raft enters the atrium, and the current becomes chaotic — swirling, splitting, dividing.

works.title: Passage 4
works.description:
The Blue‑Born try to hold onto each other, but the bloodstream does not allow it.

One by one, they are swept into different chambers, different arteries, different destinies. Their hands slip. Their voices vanish. Their faces disappear into the rushing red.

There is no time for goodbye.  
There is no ceremony for separation.  
The body simply moves them on.

This is the truth of the Heartstream:

No one stays together.  
Everyone is carried away.  
Life is a river that never lets you hold what you love for long.

* The Multiplying World — infinite possibility, fractal nature of reality.  
* The Lost Tether — the cup as a symbol of grounding and identity.  
* The Being of Circles and Crescents — subconscious intelligence, inner guide.  
* The Loop of Fear — the mind confronting its own fragility.  
* The Reemergence of Beauty — resilience, surrender, and acceptance.  
Creative Applications  
This Vision can be used as:  
* A mythic origin for a character’s awakening.  
* A symbolic map for journeys into the subconscious.  
* A template for visionary experiences in narrative worlds.  
* A psychological trial or rite of passage.  
* A metaphysical encounter with an archetypal guide.  
Legacy  
The Vision of July Fourteenth stands as a record of transformation—a moment when perception expanded, fractured, and reassembled into something new. It preserves the emotional truth of the experience without glorifying or encouraging the circumstances that produced it. Its value lies in its symbolism, its narrative potential, and its insight into the depths of the human mind.

The Architecture of Being

The Weight of Being Human  
	Don’t fear the inevitable. It seems simple enough, but that includes death, heartbreak, and every uncomfortable threshold we’d rather avoid. We are simple creatures, if you consider our chaos simplicity. For that’s what we are — chaos. We adapt, overcome, and change when faced with any challenge or adversity.  
	And beneath all that movement lies a single truth: humanity is a creature of duality.  
To be human is to be both weak and strong, dumb and brilliant, fragile and relentless. We live suspended between opposites, and the only sane response is presence — the willingness to stand inside the tension rather than flee from it.  
	We will never eat our cake and have it too. We must either sit with hunger or want; our eyes crave the cake, our soul hungers for it — which will you feed? Desire is the compass, but deprivation is the teacher. The question is moot, however: how can you live without satiation, and how would you find the substance from which to feed yourself without craving?	
	A man doesn’t know how much he values water until he is in a desert, how much he values his family until he is alone, how much he would give to receive that which he is in want of. This is the paradox of being human: we only recognize meaning when it threatens to disappear.

The trick to being human is that we can only see the story from our own eyes; take into account the biases of the viewer and it becomes that much harder to discern fact from façade.  
	Never let your mind linger on your past — you don’t live there anymore — nor reach too far into the future, because you are not welcome there yet. The present is yours, and life a present; it only means as much as you give it meaning.  
	Think of the moment you cup your hands under cold tap water after hours in the heat — how the shock, the relief, the clarity all arrive at once. That is presence.  
You don’t water the grass for tomorrow; you water it for the day you see it green and alive. That day is only real when it is present.

works.title: Passage 2 · part 1 of 2
works.description:
The Hymn of the Living  
	Greatness isn’t about luck, wit, or grit. It’s not for the few, the holy, or the lords of vast wealth.  
Greatness is not a crown worn by the powerful, but a fire rekindled by the broken.  
	Greatness was taken from the lowest to be given to those who have all but want. Farmers, young men, and the innocent all march to the cry of a war started for the profiteers, the powerful, and the greedy. None of those who die will see the riches they bleed for, and those who they fought for will cleanse their spoils of sacrifice. Not even their families will have ease in death.  
	But greatness does not die in the trenches; it dies in the quiet rooms where no one speaks to one another anymore. For to be brought low, humbled, and left for dead is not the end of greatness—it is the beginning of it. What is greatness but to make silk of dirty rags, feasts from table scraps, and grand cathedrals out of ruined stone.  
	Think of a grandmother’s hands kneading dough in a dim kitchen, the soft rhythm of survival passed down through touch—that is greatness, not the gold on a king’s table.  
Halls filled with children’s laughter and elderly hymns are richer than all those kings have tread. But children grow up, and elders pass in the night. Greatness fades as families lose their lineage, inheritance, and history.  
	Isolation becomes the new hymn, and vanity distorts the echo.

works.title: Passage 2 · part 2 of 2
works.description:
For no one in isolation is great; greatness is born in love, devotion, and the care of others. No one given to vanity will find the peace of their own becoming, for they have traded their birthright of greatness for the hollow image of another.  
	Vanity and isolation appear to be opposites, but they are two sides of the same coin—one clinging to the eyes of others for worth, the other crushed by the mere thought of being seen. This constant question am I enough must stop being asked, answered, and overlooked.  
	How can freedom be free if we never act freely? We ask to drive but never leave the trunk. We sit in the darkness of our thoughts, blinded by the confines we built, silenced by doors we closed because it felt impossible to stand between them and their closing.  
	Our mind becomes our enemy only because we make it such a place.  
We are not meant to burn alone in the dark. Greatness begins the moment we stop setting fire to ourselves.

works.title: Passage 3 · part 1 of 2
works.description:
The Doctrine of Choice  
	You have a choice — maybe not in where you begin, or why you were placed in this life, but always in how you live it. We move through the world as if everything is outside our control, as if we are passengers in our own story, but that illusion only survives until we look closely. Life will take things from you without asking: jobs, people, certainty, comfort. You don’t choose to be fired, to lose, to be betrayed, or to feel pain. But in the moments when life strips you bare, one thing remains entirely yours: your response.  
	This is the heart of choice — not control over circumstance, but sovereignty over your becoming. You can choose peace over war, calm over panic, love over hate, and greatest of all, hope over mourning. These choices do not erase suffering, but they shape what suffering becomes. They turn wounds into wisdom, endings into thresholds, and grief into a form of knowing.  
	When my grandfather died, I refused to see it as the moment I lost him. Instead, it became the moment I finally understood him — the moment his life became a story I could hold, examine, and learn from. To shed a tear is not a choice; the body grieves on instinct. But to let the tear linger, to let it fall with intention, to allow it to bring a moment of peace rather than despair — that is a choice.

works.title: Passage 3 · part 2 of 2
works.description:
Choice is not loud. It is not dramatic. It is the quiet turning of the inner wheel. Think of the way morning light spills across a kitchen table — soft, unannounced, indifferent to your plans or your pain. You cannot summon that light or delay it, but you can choose to sit in it. You can choose to let it warm your hands, your face, your spirit. Presence is not given; it is chosen.  
	We cannot choose tomorrow, and we cannot rewrite yesterday. But we can choose the posture we take toward the present. We can choose to stand in it fully, without flinching, without running, without numbing ourselves to its weight.  
	And this is where the emotional arc of choice reveals itself:  
first awareness, then acceptance, then action.  
	Awareness that life is not ours to command. Acceptance that suffering is not a punishment. Action that transforms circumstance into meaning.  
	Life will always offer you storms, but it will also offer you the stillness between them. And in that stillness, you decide who you are becoming. Choice is the quiet architect of a life — shaping you not through grand decisions, but through the small, repeated acts of courage that no one else sees.  
	You cannot choose the world you inherit, but you can choose the world you build within it. And that is enough to change everything.

works.title: Passage 4 · part 1 of 2
works.description:
The paradox of Becoming  
	Most people never see the bigger picture of their own lives. The accumulation of their choices stays invisible until it’s too late, or until someone else points out what they’ve become. We rarely recognize the moment we step into the life we once prayed for, because becoming requires presence — and presence is the one thing we abandon most easily.  
	So many look back at their “prime” only to realize they were living in a different life entirely, one they never fully inhabited. We stay loyal to versions of ourselves that no longer exist. We keep showing up to a past that has already closed its doors. The best moment isn’t just now — the only moment is now.  
	Becoming is a strange, quiet transformation. You only become something when you stop trying to prove you’re becoming it. Identity doesn’t arrive with fanfare; it settles in like dawn light through a window — unnoticed until the room is already bright. Why do we work so hard to justify being ourselves when the only time we will ever truly be ourselves is in this exact breath?

works.title: Passage 4 · part 2 of 2
works.description:
Some people die having never felt at home in their own skin. They spend their lives trying to belong to a world that never asked them to change in the first place. I mourn for those who alter their bodies, their voices, their souls just to feel acceptable. Not because change is wrong, but because belonging built on imitation is a fragile home. You can only be yourself, no matter how hard you try to be anything else.  
	Feel pride in being one of one. There will never be another you — only replicas, echoes, approximations. Don’t become a replica. Become an original.  
	You only realize yourself when you allow yourself to be yourself. Becoming is not a performance; it is a surrender. It is the moment you stop rehearsing your life and finally step into it. The trick to becoming is forgetting you started.
